extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in the American party system and election law (early 20th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter describing the mechanics, legal regulation, and practical effects of party primaries, conventions, delegate selection, and the party 'machine' across U.S. states around the turn of the 20th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voter eligibility at primaries (open vs closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly speaking there are two systems. Under the 'Open Primary' plan the use of the so-called 'Australian' secret ballot enables the voter to vote a party primary ticket without declaring to which party he belongs... Under the 'Closed Primary' plan the voter is subjected to some test determining his party affiliation, and can vote only for the candidates of that party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Wisconsin — the primary is secret and the voter may cast his ballot as he pleases (open). California (statute of 1909) — the voter must declare the political party with which he intends to affiliate and receives only that party's ballot (closed). Minnesota — the voter must declare his allegiance. Some States require enrollment or even a pledge to support the party's nominee (Louisiana, Texas). Ballots cast for any person are counted only as that person's candidacy for the party whose ticket his name is on (prevents cross-voting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Party-controlled voter lists and membership tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Local committees usually make up regular lists of party voters entitled to participate in primaries and may exclude persons it deems not loyal members of the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usual tests: Did the claimant vote the party ticket at the last important election (presidential or governorship)? Some local rules require existing members to vote to admit newcomers, and exact pledges to obey the local committee and support party nominations; breach can lead to expulsion. Effect: three-fourths or four-fifths of party voters in an area may be kept off the lists and excluded; persons kept off may be ineligible as party candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summoning and conduct of primaries and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A township or ward primary is summoned by the local party managing committee (or permanent officer by by-laws); primaries for larger areas are summoned by the county committee. Conventions are summoned by the managing committee for the district; when sufficient delegates are present, a temporary chairman is appointed, a Committee on Credentials examines credentials, then a permanent chairman is proposed and the convention is 'organized.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure details: managing committee fixes hour/place; temporary chairman calls to order, names credentials committee, which admits duly accredited delegates; at close chairman signs list of delegates chosen and adjourns sine die. These procedural steps are standard for state and local conventions (national conventions described elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate selection procedures and credentialing
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates are selected in primaries or by local committees and proceed to conventions; their credentials are examined and admitted by a Committee on Credentials before convention business proceeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any names not accepted by general consent are voted on. At the close the chairman signs the list of delegates chosen. Delegates may be chosen from preprepared lists by the local committee or by other voters present proposing names. The credentials committee determines who is duly accredited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding of delegates and majority decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every member of a nominating meeting (primary or convention) is deemed to be bound by the vote of the majority to support the candidate whom the majority select; a delegate is generally held to bind those whom he represents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binding is often informal — enforced by 'long usage' and a sentiment of honour and party loyalty rather than legal compulsion; municipal elections show weaker obligation. The vote of a majority carries a 'sacredness' in America stronger than in Europe (per author).

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing committee control over nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: The managing committee usually prepares beforehand a list of names of persons to be chosen as delegates and who shall be proposed as candidates for party nominations; their nominees are usually adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although any delegate may propose any person, in practice those who manage the choice of delegates have already settled which candidates delegates are to support. Delegates may be instructed to 'go solid' or given ordered preference lists for major offices (A. B., failing him C. D., etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative regulation and state variation of primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes in nearly all the States deal to a greater or less extent with times and manner of holding primary meetings and with selection of delegates, but regulations vary widely and are frequently changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Range from minor provisions (dates, ballot preparation, counting methods) to sweeping measures (e.g., Oregon and Wisconsin requiring nominations at public primaries under official supervision). Oklahoma's constitution included important provisions on primary elections. By 1909 two-thirds of States had direct primaries in some form, and in 26 States U.S. Senators were practically nominated by the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official supervision and administration of primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of primaries is generally placed under the supervision of the same regular officials who conduct elections; hours, methods, and administration are prescribed and official expenses are borne by the public authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may require separate official ballots for each party or regulate ballot colour/size. Those requiring all parties to hold primaries on same day often require same polling places and official ballot boxes. Supervision aims to regularize primaries and align them with election administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-corruption precautions at primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: For the prevention of corruption and other offences at primaries, the usual precautions against bribery and fraudulent voting at elections are prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary statutes commonly include measures similar to regular election law to prevent bribery and fraud; these are part of legislative attempts to cure abuses of the machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of primaries' use for nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which primaries are used to nominate candidates varies widely: sometimes only delegates and committee members are selected by ballot, in other cases primaries are required for many or nearly all party candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local committees may decide whether primaries are used for local offices. Laws of Wisconsin, Oregon, Nebraska and others required primaries for nomination of U.S. Senators and other officers (excluding presidential electors, certain judicial persons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity and frequency of elections as a systemic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The extraordinary number of elective offices and short terms in the U.S. produces a profusion of elections and primaries, making the system complex and burdensome to voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: voters frequently called to polls and must choose among large numbers of candidates; complexity creates need for extensive machinery and professional politicians. Examples: Chicago ballots with hundreds of names; Sioux City held multiple elections in a year; New York primaries with ballots containing 835 candidates. Complexity may undermine intended voter freedom and enable professionals to manipulate systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot design and length affecting voter capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Long and elaborately constructed ballots and complex forms of primary law can make the system so intricate that 'no one but an expert can master' it, burdening the voter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: Chicago ballot two feet two inches by eighteen and one-half inches containing 334 names; New York Democratic primary ballot containing 835 candidates; such ballot burden is discussed in Professor Beard's 'The Ballot's Burden'. Design and length are evaluated by their practical effect on voters' ability to make informed choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and attractiveness of delegate offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many delegate roles and offices are humble, unattractive, and time-consuming, men whose time is valuable will refuse the post of delegate, leaving the function to others less likely to exercise independent judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: best citizens (men of position and intelligence) rarely serve as delegates; the bulk of delegates will be persons unlikely to possess or exercise careful, independent judgment. This affects the quality of nominations and strengthens professional politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal challenges and constitutionality of primary laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Many legal questions arise and many judicial decisions have been delivered upon primary enactments when it has been alleged that provisions of a particular primary law are unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that these statutes have provoked litigation across states; specifics vary by state and statute complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding voter declarations and the tension with voter freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions requiring a voter at a primary to declare himself a member of a political party, or to bind himself to support the primary's nominee, are questionable as they may unduly limit the voter's freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such requirements were thought in some States to be needed as protection against tricks, but the author questions whether they legitimately restrict citizens (argument especially noted from a European perspective). Examples: statutes making declaration or pledge a precondition to voting (California 1909, Minnesota, Louisiana, Texas).

rubrics_metrics.name: State experimentation and reform tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: States are experimenting with different forms of legislative control over party operations; the variety gives hope that one form may ultimately be best and shows a reforming spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oregon, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Oklahoma among those that appear to have gone far; the rapid adoption of primary laws across states indicates recognition of machine evils and ongoing search for durable improvements. The author summarizes tendencies rather than providing exhaustive statutory detail.
